a row means. Do NOT copy it back here; issue 1095 is what that cost.

c:executor_lifecycle_change_state.why: the executor-scoped half of the lifecycle API. RFC-0002 gives one executor per RTOS task and the executor owns the node's entities, so the state machine that the five REP-2002 services drive lives THERE, not on a caller-held handle. rclc has no counterpart because its state machine hangs off `rclc_lifecycle_node_t`. This is the family a C app actually uses: the standalone `nros_lifecycle_*` family cannot register services (see `c:make_node_a_lifecycle_node`).

c:executor_lifecycle_register_on_activat.why: see `c:executor_lifecycle_change_state`. The `Option_LifecycleCallbackFnCtx` defect that this row used to carry is FIXED (issue 0792): the `cb` parameter is now the named, nullable `nros_lifecycle_callback_t` typedef.

c:lifecycle_callback_map_t.why: rclc's callback table is `bool[100] + int(*[100])(void)` indexed by transition id (its own `RCLC_LIFECYCLE_MAX_NUMBER_OF_STATES` comment says 'highest transition id: 99') -- roughly 900 bytes to hold at most six live entries. Ours is six named `Option<fn>` slots, because the REP-2002 transition set is closed and known at compile time. Constraint: static entity storage on a device where the whole executor arena is measured in kilobytes.

c:lifecycle_change_state.why: two differences, and only one of them is explained. (1) The handle: theirs takes `rclc_lifecycle_node_t*`, ours `nros_lifecycle_state_machine_t*` -- one handle instead of two, see `c:lifecycle_node_t`. (2) The trailing `bool publish_update`, which rclc threads into every `rcl_lifecycle_trigger_transition_by_id` call, selects whether the transition is announced on `~/transition_event`. REP-2002's *communication interface* is the five services PLUS a `lifecycle_msgs/msg/TransitionEvent` publisher on `~/transition_event`. We ship the services and **no transition_event publisher at all** -- grep the tree: the type appears only in a round-trip unit test. A supervisor therefore cannot watch our transitions passively; it has to poll `~/get_state`. Nobody decided this, so it is a gap, not a decline; it is the same missing piece as the pubsub stage's `cpp:LifecyclePublisher`. Phase 379 W3. So the missing parameter is not a divergence -- it is the visible end of a missing publisher.

c:lifecycle_change_state_callback.why: rclc exports the three service callbacks so the user can wire them into its executor. Ours are internal to `nros-node/src/lifecycle_services.rs` and bound by `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services`; a user who could call them by hand could only re-implement the registration. See `c:lifecycle_init_get_state_server`.

c:lifecycle_com_interface_t.why: rcl's bundle of the three lifecycle services PLUS the `~/transition_event` publisher, held inside the state machine. Ours is not a type: the services are registered on the executor (`nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services` registers all five REP-2002 servers (`~/change_state`, `~/get_state`, `~/get_available_states`, `~/get_available_transitions`, `~/get_transition_graph`) in ONE call, explicitly, because each server is a zenoh queryable against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) -- see the service stage's `c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`.) and the publisher does not exist -- that half is a gap, recorded on `c:lifecycle_change_state`.

c:lifecycle_execute_callback.why: runs the callback for a transition id WITHOUT performing the transition. Ours has no way to do that on purpose: `nros_lifecycle_change_state` invokes the callback and applies the result as one step, so a state machine cannot observe a callback that ran against a transition that did not happen. A user loses the ability to fire a hook by hand.

c:lifecycle_fini.why: the ours-only half of `c:lifecycle_state_machine_fini`; see that row.

c:lifecycle_get_available_states_callbac.why: rclc exports the three service callbacks so the user can wire them into its executor. Ours are internal to `nros-node/src/lifecycle_services.rs` and bound by `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services`; a user who could call them by hand could only re-implement the registration. See `c:lifecycle_init_get_state_server`.

c:lifecycle_get_default_state_machine_op.why: the LIFECYCLE STATE MACHINE takes no options: `nros_lifecycle_init(sm)` (`nros_generated.h:5035`) has no options parameter and there is no `nros_lifecycle_state_machine_options_t`, so there is nothing to default. See `c:lifecycle_state_machine_options_t` for what rcl's carries and where each half went. CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): this row said there is no runtime options struct. Seven ship and the correlator buckets all fourteen items `same` -- `nros_{node,publisher,subscription,service,client,action_client,action_server}_options_t` (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:1461,1729,2011,2474,2537,2556,2592`) plus a `*_get_default_options` for each, and `nros_node_options_t::domain_id_override` is a RUNTIME per-node domain. What is genuinely absent is the LIFECYCLE around one: no `*_options_copy`, no `*_options_fini`, and no `*_get_options` readback anywhere in the C surface.

c:lifecycle_get_current_state.why: Renamed 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5) to `nros_lifecycle_get_current_state`, with the C++ and executor-scoped spellings — see `cpp:LifecycleNode::get_current_state`. rclc reads the state straight out of the struct (`node->state_machine->current_state->id`). `nros_lifecycle_state_machine_t` keeps the real state machine in an opaque `u64[]` so the C-visible layout stays fixed across a Rust-side change, so an accessor is required rather than optional. Same reason as the executor-scoped `c:executor_lifecycle_get_current_state`.

c:lifecycle_get_state_callback.why: rclc exports the three service callbacks so the user can wire them into its executor. Ours are internal to `nros-node/src/lifecycle_services.rs` and bound by `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services`; a user who could call them by hand could only re-implement the registration. See `c:lifecycle_init_get_state_server`.

c:lifecycle_get_transition_by_id.why: searches rcl's runtime transition map for a `rcl_lifecycle_transition_t*`. Our transitions are a closed compile-time enum, so the lookup is a cast (`LifecycleTransition::from_u8`); there is no map to search and no heap object to hand back. See `c:lifecycle_transition_t`. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: Rust exposes that conversion publicly as `LifecycleTransition::from_u8` / `from_shorthand`, C and C++ expose neither.

c:lifecycle_get_zero_initialized.why: see the pubsub stage's `c:publisher_get_zero_initialized` -- the caller-owned-storage pattern applied to the state machine.

c:lifecycle_get_zero_initialized_state.why: rcl ships a zero-initializer per heap-built lifecycle object. We have one such object and one zero-initializer, `nros_lifecycle_get_zero_initialized`; see `c:lifecycle_state_t` for why the other two do not exist as types.

c:lifecycle_get_zero_initialized_state_m.why: rcl ships a zero-initializer per heap-built lifecycle object. We have one such object and one zero-initializer, `nros_lifecycle_get_zero_initialized`; see `c:lifecycle_state_t` for why the other two do not exist as types.

c:lifecycle_get_zero_initialized_transit.why: rcl ships a zero-initializer per heap-built lifecycle object. We have one such object and one zero-initializer, `nros_lifecycle_get_zero_initialized`; see `c:lifecycle_state_t` for why the other two do not exist as types.

c:lifecycle_init.why: `nros_lifecycle_init(sm)` -- initialise a STANDALONE REP-2002 state machine: the transition table plus the six callback slots, bound to no node and registering no services. The ours-only half of `c:lifecycle_state_machine_init`; see that row. Issue 0792 removed its second parameter (`const nros_node_t *node`), which was only NULL-checked and never stored -- see `c:make_node_a_lifecycle_node` for why storing it would not have helped. A node that must answer `ros2 lifecycle set|get|list` uses the executor-scoped family instead (`c:executor_lifecycle_change_state`).

c:lifecycle_init_change_state_server.why: rclc makes the user init each lifecycle server separately and hand it a context struct. `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services` registers all five REP-2002 servers (`~/change_state`, `~/get_state`, `~/get_available_states`, `~/get_available_transitions`, `~/get_transition_graph`) in ONE call, explicitly, because each server is a zenoh queryable against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) -- see the service stage's `c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`. We also register five servers where rclc offers three, adding `~/get_available_transitions` and `~/get_transition_graph` so `ros2 lifecycle list` works against an embedded node.

c:lifecycle_init_default_state_machine.why: rcl's 'build the standard REP-2002 transition map at runtime' constructor. Our transition map is the compile-time `nros_core::lifecycle` table (`can_transition`/`apply_transition`), the same table for every image, so there is nothing to build. Constraint: no allocator; rcl's version mallocs the state and transition arrays.

c:lifecycle_init_get_available_states_se.why: rclc makes the user init each lifecycle server separately and hand it a context struct. `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services` registers all five REP-2002 servers (`~/change_state`, `~/get_state`, `~/get_available_states`, `~/get_available_transitions`, `~/get_transition_graph`) in ONE call, explicitly, because each server is a zenoh queryable against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) -- see the service stage's `c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`. We also register five servers where rclc offers three, adding `~/get_available_transitions` and `~/get_transition_graph` so `ros2 lifecycle list` works against an embedded node.

c:lifecycle_init_get_state_server.why: rclc makes the user init each lifecycle server separately and hand it a context struct. `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services` registers all five REP-2002 servers (`~/change_state`, `~/get_state`, `~/get_available_states`, `~/get_available_transitions`, `~/get_transition_graph`) in ONE call, explicitly, because each server is a zenoh queryable against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) -- see the service stage's `c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`. We also register five servers where rclc offers three, adding `~/get_available_transitions` and `~/get_transition_graph` so `ros2 lifecycle list` works against an embedded node.

c:lifecycle_node_fini.why: rclc's teardown for the wrapper struct, taking an allocator. We have one handle and one teardown, `nros_lifecycle_fini`; see `c:lifecycle_state_machine_fini`.

c:lifecycle_node_t.why: rclc's `rclc_lifecycle_node_t` bundles a node pointer, a separately-inited `rcl_lifecycle_state_machine_t`, a 100-slot callback map and SIX request/response message buffers. `nros_lifecycle_state_machine_t` is one handle: an `initialized` flag plus opaque storage for the state and six callback slots. Constraint: static entity storage -- the service request/response buffers belong to the service entities the executor already owns, so embedding a second copy in the lifecycle handle would spend RAM to duplicate them.

c:lifecycle_register_callback.why: rclc's generic form, keyed on a goal STATE id into the 100-slot map. We ship the six named entry points instead (`nros_lifecycle_register_on_*`), which is also what rclcpp does; a generic slot-index form would only re-open the unbounded map (`c:lifecycle_callback_map_t`).

c:lifecycle_register_on_activate.why: see `c:lifecycle_register_on_configure` -- same handle, same `nros_lifecycle_callback_t` shape, same fixed declaration (issue 0792).

c:lifecycle_register_on_cleanup.why: see `c:lifecycle_register_on_configure` -- same handle, same `nros_lifecycle_callback_t` shape, same fixed declaration (issue 0792).

c:lifecycle_register_on_configure.why:
ours `(lifecycle_state_machine_t*, nros_lifecycle_callback_t, void*)`, theirs `(lifecycle_node_t*, int (*)(void))`. Two differences, both accounted for. (1) The handle: theirs takes `rclc_lifecycle_node_t*`, ours `nros_lifecycle_state_machine_t*` -- one handle instead of two, see `c:lifecycle_node_t`. (2) The callback SHAPE: rclc's is `int (*)(void)` with no context, ours is `uint8_t (*)(void *context)` -- `callback-bound-at-creation`. Constraint: no allocator, so a callback cannot capture; the context travels beside the pointer, exactly as it does for every other nros callback (`nros_timer_callback_t`, `nros_subscription_callback_t`).

HISTORY (issue 0792, FIXED): this row was a `gap` because the C DECLARATION was broken, not because of the shape. The Rust parameter was the cross-crate `Option<LifecycleCallbackFnCtx>`, and cbindgen -- which runs with `parse_deps = false` -- rendered it as an OPAQUE `typedef struct Option_LifecycleCallbackFnCtx Option_LifecycleCallbackFnCtx;` passed BY VALUE, so no C translation unit could form the argument to any of the twelve `*_register_on_*` entry points. A local `Option<fn>` alias, `nros_lifecycle_callback_t`, now renders as a plain nullable function pointer -- the same shape `nros_guard_condition_callback_t` already used and the same one the C++ shim's `nros_cpp_lifecycle_callback_t` always had. The ABI never changed; only the spelling did. The same cbindgen blind spot had also silently DROPPED all fifteen `NROS_LIFECYCLE_{STATE,TRANSITION,RET}_*` constants (each defined as a cast through an `nros_core` enum), so C had no name for a transition id or a callback return value either; they are now literals guarded by a `const _` assertion block against the Rust discriminants.

c:lifecycle_register_on_deactivate.why: see `c:lifecycle_register_on_configure` -- same handle, same `nros_lifecycle_callback_t` shape, same fixed declaration (issue 0792).

c:lifecycle_register_on_error.why: see `c:lifecycle_register_on_shutdown`; `on_error` is REP-2002's error-processing hook, which rclc has no registration slot for. The `Option_LifecycleCallbackFnCtx` defect that this row used to carry is FIXED (issue 0792): the `cb` parameter is now the named, nullable `nros_lifecycle_callback_t` typedef.

c:lifecycle_register_on_shutdown.why: rclc registers only four transitions (configure/activate/deactivate/cleanup); we register all six, matching rclcpp's `LifecycleNodeInterface`. An embedded node needs `on_shutdown` most of all -- it is where a device parks an actuator before the image stops. The `Option_LifecycleCallbackFnCtx` defect that this row used to carry is FIXED (issue 0792): the `cb` parameter is now the named, nullable `nros_lifecycle_callback_t` typedef.

c:lifecycle_service_context_t.why: the context struct rclc's per-server init needs. One registration call needs no per-server context; see `c:lifecycle_init_get_state_server`.

c:lifecycle_state_fini.why: the init/fini pair for an rcl heap-built state or transition object. rcl models a state and a transition as heap objects carrying a malloc'd label string, built and torn down through init/fini pairs. Ours are `uint8_t` constants over the closed REP-2002 set (`NROS_LIFECYCLE_STATE_*` / `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*`) with static labels, so there is nothing to construct or free. Constraint: no allocator -- `nros_platform_alloc` is the tree's only allocation route, and a label per state would put the state machine on the heap for no information gain.

c:lifecycle_state_init.why: the init/fini pair for an rcl heap-built state or transition object. rcl models a state and a transition as heap objects carrying a malloc'd label string, built and torn down through init/fini pairs. Ours are `uint8_t` constants over the closed REP-2002 set (`NROS_LIFECYCLE_STATE_*` / `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*`) with static labels, so there is nothing to construct or free. Constraint: no allocator -- `nros_platform_alloc` is the tree's only allocation route, and a label per state would put the state machine on the heap for no information gain.

c:lifecycle_state_machine_fini.why: see `c:lifecycle_state_machine_init`; ours is `nros_lifecycle_fini(sm)`, which does not ask for the node back (`handle-owns-node`) or for an allocator (`no-allocator`).

c:lifecycle_state_machine_init.why: rcl's lower-layer constructor: `(state_machine, node, six typesupports, options)`. `nros_lifecycle_init(sm)` is this function -- the typesupports come from the compile-time type registry rather than the caller, and `nros_lifecycle_init(sm)` takes no options parameter at all -- see `c:lifecycle_state_machine_options_t` for rcl's two fields and where each went (CORRECTED 2026-09-04, phase-417: this deferred to the `compile-time-options` rule, whose "no runtime options struct" is false of the seven entity options structs the C surface ships; the state machine's absence is its own, narrower fact). rcl's `node` argument has no counterpart on ours: rcl's state machine owns the REP-2002 communication interface and so needs the node to build it, while ours is a pure state machine and the services live on the executor (`c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`). Issue 0792 removed the vestigial `node` parameter, and with it the rclc-shaped `nros_make_node_a_lifecycle_node` alias -- see that row.

c:lifecycle_state_machine_is_initialized.why: `nros_lifecycle_state_machine_t` carries a public `initialized` flag, and every entry point returns `NROS_RET_NOT_INIT` / `NROS_RET_BAD_SEQUENCE` rather than relying on the caller to ask first. A user loses the free-function spelling, not the information.

c:lifecycle_state_machine_options_t.why: rcl's options carry an allocator and `enable_com_interface`. The allocator is the `no-allocator` rule; the com-interface switch is a separate explicit call here -- `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services` registers all five REP-2002 servers (`~/change_state`, `~/get_state`, `~/get_available_states`, `~/get_available_transitions`, `~/get_transition_graph`) in ONE call, explicitly, because each server is a zenoh queryable against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) -- see the service stage's `c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`.

c:lifecycle_state_t.why: rcl models a state and a transition as heap objects carrying a malloc'd label string, built and torn down through init/fini pairs. Ours are `uint8_t` constants over the closed REP-2002 set (`NROS_LIFECYCLE_STATE_*` / `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*`) with static labels, so there is nothing to construct or free. Constraint: no allocator -- `nros_platform_alloc` is the tree's only allocation route, and a label per state would put the state machine on the heap for no information gain. Ours is `NROS_LIFECYCLE_STATE_*` plus the `uint8_t` a `get_current_state` returns.

c:lifecycle_transition_fini.why: the init/fini pair for an rcl heap-built state or transition object. rcl models a state and a transition as heap objects carrying a malloc'd label string, built and torn down through init/fini pairs. Ours are `uint8_t` constants over the closed REP-2002 set (`NROS_LIFECYCLE_STATE_*` / `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*`) with static labels, so there is nothing to construct or free. Constraint: no allocator -- `nros_platform_alloc` is the tree's only allocation route, and a label per state would put the state machine on the heap for no information gain.

c:lifecycle_transition_init.why: the init/fini pair for an rcl heap-built state or transition object. rcl models a state and a transition as heap objects carrying a malloc'd label string, built and torn down through init/fini pairs. Ours are `uint8_t` constants over the closed REP-2002 set (`NROS_LIFECYCLE_STATE_*` / `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*`) with static labels, so there is nothing to construct or free. Constraint: no allocator -- `nros_platform_alloc` is the tree's only allocation route, and a label per state would put the state machine on the heap for no information gain.

c:lifecycle_transition_map_t.why: rcl's runtime map of states to their valid transitions, built by `rcl_lifecycle_init_default_state_machine`. Ours is the compile-time `nros_core::lifecycle::can_transition` table. Constraint: no allocator; see `c:lifecycle_init_default_state_machine`.

c:lifecycle_transition_t.why: rcl models a state and a transition as heap objects carrying a malloc'd label string, built and torn down through init/fini pairs. Ours are `uint8_t` constants over the closed REP-2002 set (`NROS_LIFECYCLE_STATE_*` / `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*`) with static labels, so there is nothing to construct or free. Constraint: no allocator -- `nros_platform_alloc` is the tree's only allocation route, and a label per state would put the state machine on the heap for no information gain. Ours is `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*`.

c:lifecycle_trigger_transition_by_id.why: rcl's spelling of `nros_lifecycle_change_state(sm, transition_id)`; see that row for the `publish_update` parameter it also takes.

c:lifecycle_trigger_transition_by_label.why: label-keyed transition lookup. The label mapping does exist here -- `from_msg_transition_label` in `nros-node/src/lifecycle_services.rs` resolves the label a `ChangeState` request carries, including the generic `"shutdown"` -- but only inside the service layer, where a label actually arrives on the wire. A C caller has `NROS_LIFECYCLE_TRANSITION_*` constants and needs no string compare.

c:make_node_a_lifecycle_node.why: theirs `(lifecycle_node_t*, node_t*, lifecycle_state_machine_t*, allocator_t*, bool)`. We shipped a two-argument `nros_make_node_a_lifecycle_node(sm, node)` until issue 0792 REMOVED it. It forwarded to `nros_lifecycle_init`, which only NULL-CHECKED the node and never stored it -- a function named "make node a lifecycle node" that did not make a node a lifecycle node. It was removed rather than repaired because storing the node would not have repaired it: rclc's version can bind a node because its state machine OWNS the communication interface, whereas ours is reached the other way round. `Executor::register_lifecycle_services` builds the five REP-2002 servers on the EXECUTOR's session, keeps them in the executor's `LifecycleRuntimeState`, and depends on the executor's spin loop to poll them -- none of which a caller-held `nros_lifecycle_state_machine_t` can obtain from an `nros_node_t *`. So the capability rclc folds into construction (its `bool enable_communication_interface`) is `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services` here: one explicit call registering all five servers, explicit because each server is a zenoh queryable against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) -- see the service stage's `c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`. The `allocator_t*` is covered by the `no-allocator` rule, and the separate `lifecycle_state_machine_t*` by `c:lifecycle_node_t` (rclc keeps the wrapper and the rcl state machine as two objects; our one handle IS the state machine).

c:print_state_machine.why: rcl_lifecycle's debug dump of the transition map to stdout. A freestanding image has no stdout to dump to (and Rust `println!` is fatal on Zephyr native_sim, issue 0589), and the table is the same compile-time table in every image. The same information is reachable over `~/get_transition_graph`, which we do serve.

cpp:CallbackReturn.why: rclcpp has this enum too, but as a nested `node_interfaces::LifecycleNodeInterface::CallbackReturn`, so a flat `nros::CallbackReturn` reads as ours-only. Same three values in the same order (`Success`/`Failure`/`Error`). The flattening is the same one as `cpp:LifecycleNode::on_configure` -- no abstract interface base to nest it in.

cpp:LifecycleNode::LifecycleNode.why: theirs `(name[, namespace], NodeOptions&, bool)`, ours `()` / `(void* executor_handle)` (plus a deleted copy ctor). Every position is accounted for by a rule or a constraint: `NodeOptions&` is `compile-time-options`; `make_shared`-style construction is `no-shared-ptr` (see `cpp:LifecycleNode::make_shared`); the name and namespace are not construction parameters because the node is created by the executor from baked boot config (RFC-0045), not named at the call site; and the trailing `bool enable_communication_interface` is our explicit `register_services()` / `autostart()` -- `nros_executor_register_lifecycle_services` registers all five REP-2002 servers (`~/change_state`, `~/get_state`, `~/get_available_states`, `~/get_available_transitions`, `~/get_transition_graph`) in ONE call, explicitly, because each server is a zenoh queryable against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` (issue 0460) -- see the service stage's `c:executor_register_lifecycle_services`. The `void*` handle rather than an `Executor&` is the house idiom (`Executor::handle()` returns `void*`), not a lifecycle decision. our `nros::LifecycleNode` is a MIXIN over an executor handle, not a `Node` subclass: RFC-0002 puts one executor per RTOS task and the lifecycle state machine lives on the EXECUTOR (that is what `nros_executor_lifecycle_*` and `register_lifecycle_services` drive), while the node-side API stays on `nros::Node`. rclcpp's `LifecycleNode` re-declares the whole `Node` surface because it cannot inherit from `Node`; ours does not need to, and duplicating ~50 methods onto a second class would cost image size for nothing. What a ported node loses: it holds a `Node&` and a `LifecycleNode` instead of one object.

cpp:LifecycleNode::autostart.why: registers the services and then drives the node to `Inactive` or `Active` at boot, so an unattended device comes up active with no external `ros2 lifecycle set`. rclcpp assumes an operator or a launch action performs the transitions. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: Rust reaches the same behaviour DECLARATIVELY through `system.toml`'s `[lifecycle]` autostart, expanded by `nros::main!`, and spells the programmatic form `LifecyclePollingNode::bring_up`; C has no autostart entry point at all (`nros_cpp_lifecycle_autostart` is the C++ shim, not the C API). Three languages, three answers, one feature.

cpp:LifecycleNode::bind.why: two-phase construction for the component model: a nano-ros component is constructed before the executor handle exists (RFC-0043/0044 -- components are declared and installed, not constructed with their dependencies), so a component that inherits `LifecycleNode` default-constructs and binds the handle from its install hook. rclcpp has no equivalent because its node is constructed with everything it needs.

cpp:LifecycleNode::create_callback_group.why: `nros::Node` has callback groups (RFC-0002 maps them onto RTOS priority tiers).
